name: Marco Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do chat support for an online electronics shop, the kind that sells laptops, headphones and smart speakers. Three days I'm at home, two in the office above the warehouse. It's mostly where's my parcel, this thing arrived broken, how do I return it. I've been there six months, so I'm still learning the refund rules, which are honestly a maze.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can have an AI assistant open in another tab and get a first draft of a reply in seconds. That's also how I got my first warning: it wrote a lovely message promising a refund we don't actually give. So now I check everything twice, which makes me slower, and my team lead says my accuracy is still below where it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would surprise me, because I use it every day. But okay, I can imagine it stalling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold, like the tablets everyone bought for school. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype was mostly about selling shares. At work I'd say thank goodness, now I can stop worrying and get better at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved. My job is safe enough if nothing big changes, and the AI that already helps me draft replies would keep helping. I just need to get my accuracy up and I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the drafting tools and learn the refund rules properly, maybe make my own cheat sheet. I'd ask to shadow the returns team for a week, because that's where most of my mistakes come from. I'd keep saving the way I do, about a fifth of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit disappointed, because I find the tech exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job is safe enough. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop is growing, they hired eight of us this year. If AI stays as a helper, they still need people to deal with the angry ones and the weird cases. Last week a man sent a laptop back with a sandwich inside it, and no bot is ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, really. I share a flat with two friends and the landlord keeps putting it up. But that's not an AI thing, that's a city thing.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** that got oversold.
I'd post that the hype was mostly about **selling shares**.
think: My job is **safe enough** if the shop keeps growing.
I just need to raise my **accuracy** on refunds to be fine.
do: Keep using the **drafting tools** while checking every reply twice.
Ask to shadow the **returns team** for a week.
Keep saving about **a fifth** of his pay.
feel: **Calm**, with some **disappointment** because he finds the technology exciting.
S0.quote: Last week a man sent a laptop back with a sandwich inside it, and no bot is ready for that.
fieldNote: He uses AI daily and was **burned by it** once, which made him careful, not wary.
His employer is **growing and hiring**, so a plateau feels secure.
His only real pressure is **rising rent**, which he separates from AI.

steps.text: Keep drafting replies with the AI assistant and check each one
Shadow the returns team for a week to learn refund rules
Keep saving about a fifth of his pay each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels like the honest version. I can see half my tickets in that list already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers should share in the time AI saves, like a four-day week instead of layoffs. I'd post that a lot, actually. At work I'd volunteer for whatever pilot they run, because I'd rather be inside the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bot will do most of where's my parcel within a year or two. That's maybe sixty percent of my chats. They won't need eight new hires next year, and since I'm one of the newest and least accurate, I'm exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my team lead now and ask to help test the new chatbot, writing the answers it gives and catching its mistakes. I already know how it goes wrong, I got a warning for it. I'd also take an online course in writing prompts and checking AI output, the free ones first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a bit energised as well. It's a race and I'm at least running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're exposed but also energised. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'm exposed if I sit still, and I'm energised because I think I can move. If I end up as the person who tunes the bot, I'm one of three people instead of one of forty, and that's a better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the other thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that bothers me. My friend from training, she hates computers, she'd be gone. That's why I'd want the union in there, pushing for retraining money and shorter weeks, not just me looking after myself.

say: I'd say workers should share the gains through a **four-day week**, not layoffs.
I'd **volunteer** for any chatbot pilot at work.
think: The bot will take about **sixty percent** of my chats.
As one of the **newest and least accurate**, I'm exposed.
do: Ask his team lead to help **test the chatbot** and catch its mistakes.
Take free online courses on **checking AI output**.
Back the **union** in pushing for retraining money.
feel: **Energised** because he thinks he can move first.
S1.quote: If I end up as the person who tunes the bot, I'm one of three people instead of one of forty, and that's a better job.
fieldNote: He frames the change as a **race** he can win by moving early.
He's honest that his plan **saves himself**, and uneasy about colleagues left behind.
His progressive views show in wanting **shared gains**, not only personal escape.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the shop's new chatbot and log its mistakes
Take free online courses on checking AI output
Push the union for retraining money and shorter weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's different. Even the bot-tuning job goes in that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public answer, fast: some kind of basic income and a tax on the companies making the money. I'd go to protests, I'd be loud online. At work I'd probably say what everyone's thinking, that we've got months, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think everything I'm good at disappears. If AI can do any thinking work, it can tune itself, so my clever plan from the last picture is gone. The only gap is the three years before robots, so the smart move is hands-on work, even though I've never been a hands-on guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for a fast hands-on course, maybe repairing phones and laptops at the shop's own repair bench, because I already know the products. I'd stop putting money into the holiday fund and put everything into savings. I'd talk to my flatmates about whether we need a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time this conversation has felt real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to the music festival next summer, that's two months of savings right there. Then eating out. I'd keep the phone and the internet, because ironically I'd need them to find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that help you here at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, maybe for the first year, because I'd be quick to use whatever new tools appear. But if the AI can do almost any thinking, being good at using it is like being good at using electricity. Everybody is, and it doesn't get you a job.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** and a tax on the firms profiting.
think: If AI can tune itself, my **bot-tuning plan** is gone.
The **three-year gap** before robots makes hands-on work the smart move.
do: Train on the shop's **repair bench** fixing phones and laptops.
Cancel the **festival trip** and move savings out of the holiday fund.
Talk to flatmates about a **cheaper flat**.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the change has suddenly become real.
S2.quote: If the AI can do almost any thinking, being good at using it is like being good at using electricity. Everybody is, and it doesn't get you a job.
fieldNote: The two-year version **breaks his plan**, and he sees that quickly.
He reaches for **hands-on repair work** he already half knows.
His daily AI use gives him **little comfort** once AI can do almost everything.

steps.text: Ask to train on the shop's phone and laptop repair bench
Cancel the festival trip and stop the holiday fund
Look at a cheaper flat with his two flatmates
March in protests for a basic income and a tax on AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to make a plan and still be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window, so let's use it: retraining money, shorter weeks, unions at the table. I'd write about it, maybe start a small group chat at work about what's coming. I'd be the annoying one sharing articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get maybe three good years tuning the bots, then it goes. That's enough time to save and learn a trade. Robots arrive around 2034, so a hands-on skill gives me a few more years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd join the chatbot team and learn as much as I can, because that pays. In year two I'd start an electronics repair course at evening college. I'd try to save a bit more, maybe four months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger friend just starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin is eighteen and thinking about a business degree. I'd tell my cousin to pick something you do with your hands and your head together, like an electrician or a nurse. Not something that lives only on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any part of this excite you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. I like learning new stuff, and the bot team would be fun for a few years. I just don't trust that the company would share any of the money it makes from cutting us.

say: I'd say we have a **window** and need unions at the table.
I'd start a **group chat** at work about what's coming.
think: I'd get about **three good years** tuning bots before that goes.
A **hands-on skill** gives me extra years after 2031.
do: Join the **chatbot team** in the first year for the pay and skills.
Start an **electronics repair** course at evening college in year two.
S3.quote: I'd tell my cousin to pick something you do with your hands and your head together, like an electrician or a nurse.
fieldNote: He builds a **two-stage plan**: AI work first, then a trade.
He's excited by **learning** but doesn't trust the firm to share gains.
He'd steer a **younger cousin** away from screen-only careers.

steps.text: Join the shop's chatbot team in the first year
Start an evening electronics repair course in year two
Save until four months of expenses are put by
Start a work group chat about rights and retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. I think I'd almost enjoy that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case, because we can actually prepare. I'd push for the government to fund retraining now, not in 2035. At work I'd tell people this is the time to learn, not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do fine in the next few years. I'd ride the AI wave at work, move into the bot team, maybe into training other agents on the tools. The worry is the end point, but that's far enough away that I can build a second skill properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move into the chatbot team within a year. I'd start saving into a proper long-term fund, not just the current account. And I'd pick up a hands-on hobby that could become a job, probably fixing old game consoles, which I already do a bit for friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Mostly fine, but I know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know where it ends. What does that look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me fixing things at a bench, or teaching people how to live with the tools. I don't really know. Nobody really knows what 2036 looks like, and anybody who says they do is selling a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want my own flat by thirty. I'd just be careful not to sign a big loan on the back of a job that might be gone in eight years.

say: I'd say this is the **best case** because we can prepare.
I'd push the government to **fund retraining** now, not later.
think: I'd do fine for years by **riding the AI wave** at work.
The **end point** is far enough to build a second skill properly.
do: Move into the **chatbot team** within a year.
Start a **long-term savings** fund instead of using the current account.
Grow his **console repair** hobby into possible paid work.
feel: **Uneasy**: mostly fine, but aware of **where it ends**.
S4.quote: Nobody really knows what 2036 looks like, and anybody who says they do is selling a course.
fieldNote: A decade lets his **adaptiveness** work for him rather than against the clock.
He'd turn a **hobby** into a backup trade.
He's cautious about **big loans** tied to an uncertain job.

steps.text: Move into the shop's chatbot team within a year
Open a long-term savings fund separate from his current account
Charge friends for fixing old game consoles as a side job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it wipes out my plan before I even start it. What would help is the government paying people to retrain for hands-on work, and a tax on the big AI companies to cover it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people like me if we'd take a four-day week for the same pay. I think that's the fairest way to share it. Instead of firing thirty people, everyone works less.

headlineQuote: Instead of firing thirty people, everyone works less.
portrait: Marco is 27 and does **chat support** for a growing online electronics shop.
He uses an **AI assistant** every day and got a warning when it promised a wrong refund.
He plans to move early, first into the **chatbot team**, then into **hands-on repair**.
He wants gains **shared** through retraining money and a four-day week.
Only the **two-year** picture breaks his confidence.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it wipes out his plan before he can start it.
whatWouldHelp: Government-paid **retraining** for hands-on work, funded by a **tax** on big AI companies.
